m1.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 9:1
m1.note: MT Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 9:1–4 formalizes the three-day prohibition developed here into a systematic list of prohibited commercial activities (selling, buying, lending, renting). The Commentary concentrates on the talmudic reasoning — explaining why three days before the festival was the threshold — while the MT shifts entirely to prescriptive categories. A significant addition appears in MT 9:14: the three-day prohibition is explicitly classified as rabbinic rather than biblical, a jurisprudential distinction Rambam does not foreground in the Commentary.

m4.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 9:8
m4.note: The Commentary's ruling on commercial dealings on the festival day itself (as opposed to the pre-festival period) is codified in MT 9:8, which extends the prohibition beyond mere sale to all forms of economic benefit. Rambam also folds the Sages' distinction between permanent and temporary commerce into MT 9:13, where it becomes a formal halakhic category. The Commentary's discursive treatment of the underlying rationale (preventing participation in the idolater's joy) drops out in the MT's laconic ruleset.

m1.note: The Commentary's explanation of the cheese prohibition (gevinat akum) appears in condensed form in MT Hilkhot Maakhalot Asurot 3:13–15. Rambam's Commentary emphasizes the rabbinic rationale — cheese was forbidden because of intermarriage concerns or contact with unclean rennet — and notes the dispute among Geonim. The MT simply states the prohibition without engaging the rationale debate, illustrating Rambam's deliberate separation of the Commentary's explanatory mode from the MT's legislative mode.

m3.note: The prohibition on hides of idolaters found with a triangular incision (indicating sacrifice) is codified in MT Hilkhot Maakhalot Asurot 7:4. The Commentary explains the halakhic reasoning (the incision is a recognized sign of libation sacrifice) and notes the minority opinion permitting the hides; MT 7:4 records the ruling in favor of prohibition without retaining the dissenting position.

m6.note: The bread of idolaters (pat akum) ruling in the Commentary is codified in MT Hilkhot Maakhalot Asurot 17:12, where Rambam records the lenient position: bread baked by an idolater's baker — as opposed to a private household — is permitted where no Jewish bread is available. The Commentary here treats this as a straightforward application of rabbinic leniency; MT 17:12 frames it within a broader taxonomy of bread-baking contexts.

m1.sefaria_ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part III 29
m1.note: The talismanic (ṭilasm) images described here — fashioned at astrologically precise moments to concentrate stellar influence — appear as the organizing example of Sabian practice throughout Guide III:29–37. In the Commentary, Rambam identifies these images halakhically: do they constitute 'idols' that require burial or may they be destroyed? In the Guide, he identifies them historically-philosophically: they are the origin-point of the biblical prohibition of idolatry, crafted by the Sabians who identified the planets as intermediaries between God and humanity. The two texts are complementary apparatus: Commentary identifies the offense, Guide traces its historical root and explains why God prohibited it.

m1.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 3:11
m1.note: MT Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 3:11 codifies the ruling developed from this mishnah: a figure made in the form of a servant of the sun holding a ball or staff — i.e., exactly the ṭilasm-type image the Commentary discusses — is forbidden for benefit. The MT's laconic formulation preserves the ruling while stripping the Sabian-astral-magic context entirely; that explanatory register belongs to the Guide.

m2.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 3:10
m2.note: MT 3:10 records the prohibition on possessing images of the sun, moon, and dragon derived from this mishnah. The Commentary explains the Sages' reasoning: these were the most universally worshipped objects in antiquity. The MT simply states the categorical prohibition without retaining this anthropological context, which Rambam developed more fully in his Guide treatment of Sabian star-worship (III:29).

m3.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 7:2
m3.note: The ruling on accessories of idols (mashmeshot) — items that serve the idol but are not the idol itself — appears in MT Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 7:2–3. The Commentary draws the analogy to ritual furnishings of the Temple to explain why these accessories are prohibited; the MT retains the ruling but drops the Temple-analogy framework. Note that MT 7:6 adds a case not discussed in this mishnah: items attached to the idol at the time of manufacture are forbidden ab initio, not merely after the idol is completed.

m5.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 7:7
m5.note: The ruling on an oven built with images that were worshipped is recorded in MT Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 7:7. Rambam rules here that the oven itself becomes forbidden if the images embedded in it were worshipped; the MT codifies this and adds that the oven must be broken and rebuilt. The Commentary's fuller discussion of the majority-minority opinion dispute on this question is compressed into the MT's single ruling without attribution.

m7.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 6:6
m7.note: The prohibition on prostrating oneself on a figured stone floor, derived here from Lev. 26:1, is codified in MT Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 6:6. The Commentary explains the underlying prohibition — prostration with outstretched arms and legs was the characteristic posture of Sabian star-worship — and notes the halakhic implication: a plain stone floor (without figures) is permitted in the Temple even though it is forbidden in the provinces. The MT retains the Temple exception but strips the Sabian anthropological explanation.

m7.sefaria_ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part III 29
m7.note: The prostration prohibition discussed here (Lev. 26:1) appears in Guide III:29 as part of Rambam's Sabian-origin hypothesis for biblical law: the full-body prostration on figured stone was a Sabian star-worship posture, and God prohibited it precisely because of this pagan association. The Commentary identifies the halakhic case; the Guide locates it in the history of idolatry and provides the philosophical rationale for why God singled out this particular posture for prohibition.

m1.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 8:1
m1.note: MT Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 8:1–5 systematizes the nullification (bittul) doctrine the Commentary develops here. The Commentary's key philosophical contribution — that only an idolater can nullify an idol because worship confers a kind of ontological status on the object that only the original worshipper can revoke — surfaces as a formal rule in MT 8:9: a Jew cannot nullify an idol, only an idolater can. The Commentary preserves the reasoning; the MT records only the conclusion.

m4.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 8:9
m4.note: The case of the idol that was sold, leased, or pledged as collateral by its idolater-owner is codified in MT Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 8:9–10. The Commentary explains that sale and pledge demonstrate the idolater's contempt for his idol and therefore constitute retroactive nullification; the MT retains this ruling and adds the principle that any act demonstrating contempt (bizzayon) effectuates nullification. MT 8:11 further extends the rule to an idolater who asked a Jew to take his idol as a pledge — not in the Commentary.

m5.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 8:11
m5.note: The Commentary's discussion of specific acts that effectuate bittul — defacing, selling to a Jew, giving as a pledge — is codified in MT 8:9–12. An interesting development: the Commentary treats the question whether defacement alone is sufficient; the MT in 8:12 adds a new criterion not clearly in the mishnah or the Commentary — that the idolater must have voluntarily caused the defacement, not had it imposed by force. This is a Maimonidean addition to the halakhah.

m8.sefaria_ref: Mishneh Torah, Foreign Worship and Customs of the Nations 8:6
m8.note: The case of libation vessels and incense vessels — whether they are forbidden for benefit along with the idol — appears in MT Hilkhot Avodah Zarah 8:6. The Commentary rules that these vessels acquire the idol's forbidden status only if they were designated for idolatrous use; the MT codifies this as a general principle (MT 8:4) before applying it to specific vessel types. An important variant: the Commentary permits benefit from leftover incense if it was never actually burned before idols; MT 8:6 is silent on this question.

m1.note: MT Hilkhot Maakhalot Asurot 11:1–7 preserves the two-tier distinction Rambam draws here between yayin nesekh (wine explicitly used in idolatrous libation, biblically forbidden with no permitted benefit) and stam yeinam (ordinary wine handled by an idolater, rabbinically forbidden for consumption but permitted for benefit in certain opinions). The Commentary is unusually expansive in justifying the rabbinic decree: Rambam stresses that stam yeinam was forbidden to prevent intermarriage, not because of libation concerns per se. MT 11:7 alludes to this rationale briefly but without the Commentary's sustained argument.

m2.note: The cases of wine found in the possession of an idolater versus wine that a Jew left with an idolater — and whether each is presumed to have been used for libation — are codified in MT 11:8–10. The Commentary explains the evidentiary logic: we assess whether the idolater had the means and motive to substitute libation wine. The MT translates this into formal presumptions without retaining the evidentiary reasoning. MT 11:10 adds a rule about wine in a shared courtyard not found in the Commentary.

m8.note: The prohibition on deriving any benefit from yayin nesekh (as opposed to stam yeinam, from which benefit is permitted under certain conditions) is codified in MT Hilkhot Maakhalot Asurot 12:1. The Commentary's analysis here focuses on what counts as 'benefit' — may one use the wine as a solvent, a dye, or fuel? The MT resolves this at 12:3 by adopting a comprehensive definition: any economic use whatsoever is forbidden, not only consumption.

m11.note: The question of whether libation wine can be nullified by mixture with kosher wine (bittul be-rov) is the subject of MT Hilkhot Maakhalot Asurot 13:1–3. The Commentary rules against nullification for yayin nesekh — unlike ordinary forbidden foods, libation wine cannot become batel be-shishim or batel be-rov because it is qualitatively significant (davar she-yesh lo matirin). MT 13:1 codifies this rule and extends it: even in a majority mixture, if even a drop of libation wine is identifiable, the entire barrel is forbidden.
